In [[mathematics]], in the study of [[fractal]]s, a '''Hutchinson operator'''<ref>{{cite journal | last=Hutchinson | first=John E. | title=Fractals and self similarity | journal=Indiana Univ. Math. J. | volume=30 | year=1981 | pages=713–747 | doi=10.1512/iumj.1981.30.30055 | issue=5 | doi-access=free }}</ref> is the collective action of a set of contractions, called an [[iterated function system]].<ref>{{cite journal | last=Barnsley | first=Michael F. | author2=Stephen Demko | title=Iterated function systems and the global construction of fractals | journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences | volume=399 | year=1985 | pages=243–275 | issue=1817 }}</ref> The [[Iterated function|iteration]] of the operator converges to a unique [[attractor]], which is the often [[self-similar]] fixed set of the operator.

==Definition==
Let <math>\{f_i : X \to X\ |\ 1\leq i \leq N\}</math> be an [[iterated function system]], or a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of [[contraction mapping|contractions]] from a [[compact set]] <math>X</math> to itself.  The operator <math>H</math> is defined over subsets <math>S\subset X</math> as

:<math>H(S) = \bigcup_{i=1}^N f_i(S).\,</math>

A key question is to describe the attractors <math>A=H(A)</math> of this operator, which are compact sets. One way of generating such a set is to start with an initial compact set <math>S_0\subset X</math> (which can be a single point, called a seed) and iterate <math>H</math> as follows

:<math>S_{n+1} = H(S_n) = \bigcup_{i=1}^N f_i(S_n) </math>

and taking the limit, the iteration converges to the attractor

:<math>A = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n . </math>

==Properties==
Hutchinson showed in 1981 the existence and uniqueness of the attractor <math>A</math>. The proof follows by showing that the Hutchinson operator is contractive on the set of compact subsets of <math>X</math> in the [[Hausdorff distance]].

The collection of functions <math>f_i</math> together with composition form a [[monoid]]. With ''N'' functions, then one may visualize the monoid as a full [[k-ary tree|N-ary tree]] or a [[Cayley tree]].
